warmup.q: Ten nodes hold 100,000 keys placed by hash mod 10. You add an eleventh node and switch to hash mod 11. About how many keys now belong to a different node?
options: About 9,100: the new node's fair share
None until a rebalance job runs
warmup.why: A key stays put only if its hash leaves the same remainder for 10 and 11. The remainders repeat every 110 numbers and agree only for 0 to 9, so 10 keys in 110 stay and about 91% move. The demo counts 91,032. About 9,100 is what a good scheme moves, and the first option is tempting because it's the right answer for every scheme in this lesson except hash mod N.

sections.h: Changing N under hash mod N moves almost every key
sections.html:
Lesson 1 placed keys with hash mod N. But N doesn't stay put. You add machines before Black Friday, replace one with a failed disk, retire old hardware. Each change of N changes the answer for most keys.

Work it out for 10 nodes going to 11. A key stays where it is only if h mod 10 equals h mod 11. Both remainders repeat every 110 numbers, and they agree only for the first 10 numbers of each cycle, 0 to 9. So 10 keys in 110 stay put, and the other 100 in 110, about 91%, move. The demo below counts 91,032 of 100,000.

Moving a key isn't free. Its bytes cross the network from the old node to the new one while both keep serving traffic. On a 3 TB cluster, 91% is 2.7 TB of copying to add one machine. The new node only needs its fair share, 1/11 of the data, about 270 GB. That's the least any scheme can move, and everything above it is waste: keys going from node 3 to node 7 when neither of them is new.

That sets the target for this lesson. Moving data between nodes is called rebalancing, and a good scheme rebalances like this when a node joins:

  • it moves about 1/(N+1) of the data, the new node's fair share;
  • everything that moves goes to the new node;
  • many old nodes share the sending, so no single disk or network link does all of it.

Lesson 2's ring gets close. With 16 tokens per node, the demo moves 10.2% of the keys, all to the new node, from 9 senders. With one token per node it moves 9.2%, all from a single sender. The next two sections cover the other designs real stores use: a fixed number of partitions, partitions that split as they grow, and partition counts that grow with the nodes. The last section covers the other half of the second map: once shards move, how does a request find them?

try.title: Count what moves when an eleventh node joins
steps: Read RebalanceDemo.kt. It places 100,000 payment keys on 10 nodes four ways: hash mod N, 1,000 fixed partitions, a ring with 1 token per node and a ring with 16. Then it adds node-11 and counts the keys whose owner changed, how many went to the new node, and how many old nodes sent them.
Predict the percentage for hash mod N, and which scheme has a single sender.
Run it from the labs folder. No Docker needed.

code.title: RebalanceDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l03.demo import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.security.MessageDigest import java.util.TreeMap fun md5(key: String): Long = ByteBuffer.wrap(MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5").digest(key.toByteArray())).long /** Ten nodes hold 100,000 payment keys. An eleventh joins. How many keys move, and who sends them? */ fun main() { val ten = (1..10).map { "node-%02d".format(it) } val eleven = ten + "node-11" val keys = (0 until 100_000).map { "pay-$it" } fun report(name: String, before: (String) -> String, after: (String) -> String) { val moved = keys.filter { before(it) != after(it) } val senders = moved.map(before).toSet().size val toNew = moved.count { after(it) == "node-11" } println("%-26s %,6d keys move (%4.1f%%), %,6d of them to node-11, sent by %2d %s" .format(name, moved.size, moved.size / 1_000.0, toNew, senders, if (senders == 1) "node" else "nodes")) } // lesson 1: node = hash mod N report("hash mod N", { ten[Math.floorMod(md5(it), 10L).toInt()] }, { eleven[Math.floorMod(md5(it), 11L).toInt()] }) // fixed partitions: 1,000 of them; a key's partition never changes, whole partitions change node val owner = Array(1_000) { ten[it % 10] } val before = owner.copyOf() var given = 0 while (given < 1_000 / 11) { // node-11 takes 90 partitions, one at a time from the busiest node val donor = ten.maxBy { n -> owner.count { it == n } } owner[owner.indices.last { owner[it] == donor }] = "node-11" given++ } val partition = { key: String -> Math.floorMod(md5(key), 1_000L).toInt() } report("1,000 fixed partitions", { before[partition(it)] }, { owner[partition(it)] }) // lesson 2: a ring with T tokens per node for (t in listOf(1, 16)) { fun ring(nodes: List<String>) = TreeMap<Long, String>().apply { nodes.forEach { n -> repeat(t) { put(md5("$n#$it"), n) } } } val r10 = ring(ten) val r11 = ring(eleven) val owner = { r: TreeMap<Long, String>, k: String -> (r.ceilingEntry(md5(k)) ?: r.firstEntry()).value } report("ring, $t token(s) per node", { owner(r10, it) }, { owner(r11, it) }) } }

try.expect:
hash mod N                 91,032 keys move (91.0%),  9,150 of them to node-11, sent by 10 nodes
1,000 fixed partitions      8,955 keys move ( 9.0%),  8,955 of them to node-11, sent by 10 nodes
ring, 1 token(s) per node   9,212 keys move ( 9.2%),  9,212 of them to node-11, sent by  1 node
ring, 16 token(s) per node 10,230 keys move (10.2%), 10,230 of them to node-11, sent by  9 nodes

hash mod N moves 91% of the keys, and only 9,150 of those 91,032 go to the new node: the rest trade places between old nodes. The other three move close to the ideal 9.1%, all of it to node-11. One token per node puts all the sending on one neighbour. Fixed partitions spread it over all ten old nodes, and the 16-token ring over nine.

sections.h: Fixed partitions: many more partitions than nodes, moved whole
sections.html:
Split lesson 1's first map in two. First, hash each key to one of P partitions with hash mod P, where P is chosen once, when the system is created, and is much bigger than the node count: say 1,000 partitions for 10 nodes. Second, keep a table from partition to node, 100 partitions each. A key's partition never changes. When an eleventh node joins, it takes whole partitions from the others until it holds its share, 90 of them, about nine from each old node. Only the keys in those 90 partitions move: 8,955 of 100,000 in the demo, the minimum, sent by all ten old nodes.

A partition is a natural unit to move. It's a set of files, or a log, that the old node can copy across while it keeps serving; then the table flips the partition's owner to the new node. The stepper walks through one join.

This is the most common design. A Kafka topic has a fixed number of partitions; the producer picks a key's partition by hashing the key mod that number, and brokers move whole partitions between them. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch fix an index's number of primary shards when you create it, and route each document with hash(_routing) % number_of_primary_shards, where _routing is the document id unless you set it. Redis Cluster has 16,384 hash slots (the Caching track's Redis Cluster lesson). Couchbase, Riak and Citus work the same way. And Notion's 480 logical shards from lesson 1 are fixed partitions over PostgreSQL: going from 32 machines to 96 moved schemas between machines, and no workspace changed shard.

Notion chose 480 because it divides evenly by many numbers. With P partitions on N nodes, the busiest node holds P/N rounded up. 480 spreads perfectly over 32, 40, 48 or 96 machines. 512 spreads perfectly only over powers of two: on 96 machines some hold 6 and some 5, and the busiest carries 13% more than the average.

The price is that P is chosen once. Too few, and you hit a wall: with 12 partitions, a 13th node has nothing to hold, and more nodes stop helping. Too many, and every partition has a fixed cost. Elastic's sizing guidance aims for shards of 10 to 50 GB, and each shard runs its part of a search on one thread, so thousands of tiny shards use up the search thread pool. Changing P later means rehashing keys. In Kafka, adding partitions changes hash mod P for most keys, so a key's new records go to a different partition from its old ones, and per-key order breaks. Elasticsearch makes you split, shrink or reindex. So pick P for the size you expect years from now, with plenty of divisors.

sections.h: Partitions that split, and the danger of moving them automatically
sections.html:
Key-range stores can't fix their partition count in advance, because a range holds whatever keys fall into it. So they split. A range that grows past a size limit is cut in two at its middle key: HBase splits a region at 10 GiB, and CockroachDB splits a range at 512 MiB. MongoDB works in ranges of about 128 MB, which its balancer splits and moves to even out data size across shards. CockroachDB also merges neighbours that shrink below 128 MiB, and splits a range that is too busy, so one hot range can be served by two nodes. The number of partitions now follows the data: a small table has a few, a big one has thousands. A split moves nothing between machines by itself. It makes a new unit that can move, and a new node takes whole ranges, as with fixed partitions.

Cassandra takes a third path: the number of partitions grows with the nodes. Each node owns 16 token ranges, so 10 nodes make 160 ranges, and an 11th node adds 16 more by splitting existing ones (lesson 2). A partition's size grows with the data per node, not with the data in total.

Who decides when to move a partition? The store can do it on its own, or it can propose a plan for a person to approve. Automatic is convenient, and it fails in one specific way. Suppose a node gets overloaded, by a hot partition say. Its replies slow down and its heartbeats arrive late, so the failure detector decides it's dead. The rebalancer moves its partitions to the survivors, which were already busy. Now they're overloaded, their heartbeats slip, and they're declared dead too. That's a cascading failure: the rebalancer itself spreads the overload. The Try-it runs it on five nodes at 88% of capacity. One partition triples, and two seconds later the automatic cluster serves nothing, while the cluster that only alerted a person still serves 4,520 of 4,840 requests a second.

So many systems keep a person in the loop for membership. Dynamo made adding and removing nodes an explicit admin command, so that a node that drops out for a few minutes doesn't trigger a flood of copying. Couchbase and Riak propose a new assignment and wait for an administrator to commit it. MongoDB's balancer is automatic but careful: a shard takes part in only one chunk migration at a time, and you can limit balancing to a window of quiet hours. For a peak you can see coming, Black Friday or a ticket sale, rebalance by hand beforehand, while the cluster is quiet.

try.title: Watch automatic rebalancing take a cluster down
steps: Read CascadeDemo.kt. Five nodes hold 20 partitions of 220 requests a second, 880 per node against a capacity of 1,000. At second 1, partition 7 on node-3 goes to 660. A node over capacity misses its health checks and is called dead. One policy moves a dead node's partitions to the least loaded survivors; the other only alerts a person.
Predict how many seconds the automatic cluster lasts.

code.title: CascadeDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l03.demo /** * Five nodes, 20 partitions of 220 requests a second each: 880 a second per node, against a capacity * of 1,000. At second 1, one merchant in partition 7 (on node-3) triples that partition's traffic. * A node over capacity answers health checks late, so the failure detector calls it dead. */ fun main() { val capacity = 1_000.0 for (automatic in listOf(true, false)) { val load = MutableList(20) { 220.0 } val owner = MutableList(20) { "node-${it % 5 + 1}" } val alive = (1..5).map { "node-$it" }.toSortedSet() println(if (automatic) "automatic: move a dead node's partitions to the others" else "manual: alert a person, move nothing") for (second in 0..3) { if (second == 1) load[7] = 660.0 // the hot merchant val perNode = alive.associateWith { n -> owner.indices.filter { owner[it] == n }.sumOf { load[it] } } val served = perNode.values.sumOf { minOf(it, capacity) } println(" second $second: %s served %,.0f of %,.0f a second".format( perNode.entries.joinToString(" ") { "${it.key}=%.0f".format(it.value) }.ifEmpty { "no nodes left" }, served, load.sum())) if (!automatic) continue val dead = perNode.filter { it.value > capacity }.keys alive -= dead if (alive.isEmpty()) continue // the "fix": hand every partition of a dead node to the least loaded survivor, one at a time for (p in owner.indices.filter { owner[it] in dead }) { owner[p] = alive.minBy { n -> owner.indices.filter { owner[it] == n }.sumOf { load[it] } } } } } }

try.expect:
automatic: move a dead node's partitions to the others
  second 0: node-1=880 node-2=880 node-3=880 node-4=880 node-5=880  served 4,400 of 4,400 a second
  second 1: node-1=880 node-2=880 node-3=1320 node-4=880 node-5=880  served 4,520 of 4,840 a second
  second 2: node-1=1100 node-2=1540 node-4=1100 node-5=1100  served 4,000 of 4,840 a second
  second 3: no nodes left  served 0 of 4,840 a second
manual: alert a person, move nothing
  second 0: node-1=880 node-2=880 node-3=880 node-4=880 node-5=880  served 4,400 of 4,400 a second
  second 1: node-1=880 node-2=880 node-3=1320 node-4=880 node-5=880  served 4,520 of 4,840 a second
  second 2: node-1=880 node-2=880 node-3=1320 node-4=880 node-5=880  served 4,520 of 4,840 a second
  second 3: node-1=880 node-2=880 node-3=1320 node-4=880 node-5=880  served 4,520 of 4,840 a second

At second 1 node-3 is over capacity and drops 320 requests a second. The automatic policy calls it dead and hands its four partitions (1,320 a second) to the other four nodes. Each was at 880, so every one of them goes over 1,000, and at second 3 the whole cluster is "dead". The manual policy keeps losing 320 a second on one node, 7% of traffic, until a person moves or splits partition 7. The model is crude (real detectors wait several seconds, and real moves take minutes of copying, which adds load), but the shape is the one real cascades have.

sections.h: Finding the shard: any node, a routing tier or a smart client
sections.html:
Partitions move, so a client can't hard-code where a key lives. Something has to hold the second map, partition to node, and every request has to consult it. The figure shows the three places to put that lookup.

Any node. The client sends the request to any node, and that node forwards it to the right one. Cassandra works this way: whichever node receives a request becomes its coordinator, and every node keeps the whole token map, spread by gossip (lesson 5 covers it). Cassandra 6.0, still at alpha, moves this map into a consensus-backed metadata service.

A routing tier. The client talks to a router that knows the map and stores no data. MongoDB's mongos caches the chunk map from the config servers (a small replica set that stores the cluster's metadata) and sends each query to the shards that hold its chunks; a query without the shard key goes to all of them. Figma's DBProxy sits between the application and PgBouncer (a connection pooler), parses each SQL query and routes it by shard key. Vitess does the same for MySQL.

A partition-aware client. The client library keeps its own copy of the map and goes straight to the owner, saving a hop. Cassandra's token-aware drivers compute the token and pick a replica. A Kafka producer fetches the cluster's metadata, which names the leader broker of each partition, and refreshes it when a broker answers that it's no longer the leader. A Redis Cluster client caches the slot map.

Wherever the lookups happen, the authoritative map has to live somewhere every party agrees on, or two routers can each believe a different node owns a partition. Many systems keep it in a consensus store, a small replicated service that changes its data only when a majority of its nodes agree: HBase in ZooKeeper, Kubernetes in etcd, Kafka in its own KRaft controllers, and CockroachDB, TiDB and ScyllaDB in built-in Raft groups. The Consistency and consensus track builds these.

Every copy of the map goes stale the moment a partition moves, so the real design question is what a node does with a request for a key it no longer owns. Redis Cluster's answer, from the Caching track, is the cleanest to study. A node that doesn't own the key's slot answers MOVED <slot> <node>: the slot lives there now, so update your map and retry. While a slot is migrating, its old owner still answers the keys it has and answers ASK <slot> <node> for keys that have already been copied. The client sends that one request to the new node, prefixed by the command ASKING, and leaves its map alone, because most of the slot is still on the old owner. When the migration ends, the old owner answers MOVED, once per client, and the maps catch up. No request fails during a migration: each one costs at most one extra hop. The lab builds that client.

try.title: Trace three reads through a slot migration
steps: Read RedirectDemo.kt. Three nodes share 16 slots; slot 0 starts on A and holds three keys. The client reads all three before the migration, after one key has been copied to C, and after the migration ends. Each line prints every hop and the client's map entry for slot 0.
Predict which reads get ASK, which get MOVED, and when the client's map changes.

code.title: RedirectDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l03.demo /** Three nodes, 16 slots. Slot 0 moves from A to C while a client keeps reading it. */ fun main() { val slotOf = { key: String -> Math.floorMod(md5(key), 16L).toInt() } val owner = Array(16) { listOf("A", "B", "C")[it * 3 / 16] } val stores = mapOf("A" to HashMap<String, String>(), "B" to HashMap(), "C" to HashMap()) val keys = (0 until 300).map { "pay-$it" }.filter { slotOf(it) == 0 }.sorted().take(3) keys.forEach { stores.getValue(owner[0])[it] = "value of $it" } var migratingTo: String? = null // the server side: what node answers to GET key fun serve(node: String, key: String, asking: Boolean): String { val slot = slotOf(key) return when { owner[slot] == node && migratingTo != null && key !in stores.getValue(node) -> "ASK $slot $migratingTo" owner[slot] == node -> "\"${stores.getValue(node)[key]}\"" migratingTo == node && asking -> "\"${stores.getValue(node)[key]}\"" else -> "MOVED $slot ${owner[slot]}" } } // the client: its own slot map; MOVED updates it, ASK doesn't val slotMap = owner.copyOf() fun get(key: String) { var node = slotMap[slotOf(key)] var asking = false val trace = StringBuilder("GET $key") while (true) { val reply = serve(node, key, asking) trace.append(" -> ${if (asking) "ASKING, " else ""}$node: $reply") val parts = reply.split(" ") when (parts[0]) { "MOVED" -> { slotMap[parts[1].toInt()] = parts[2]; node = parts[2]; asking = false } "ASK" -> { node = parts[2]; asking = true } else -> break } } println(" $trace (client map: slot 0 on ${slotMap[0]})") } println("before the migration") keys.forEach(::get) println("slot 0 starts moving to C; ${keys[0]} has been copied") migratingTo = "C" stores.getValue("C")[keys[0]] = stores.getValue("A").remove(keys[0])!! keys.forEach(::get) println("the rest are copied, and C owns slot 0") keys.drop(1).forEach { stores.getValue("C")[it] = stores.getValue("A").remove(it)!! } owner[0] = "C" migratingTo = null keys.forEach(::get) }

try.expect:
before the migration
  GET pay-103 -> A: "value of pay-103"   (client map: slot 0 on A)
  GET pay-117 -> A: "value of pay-117"   (client map: slot 0 on A)
  GET pay-159 -> A: "value of pay-159"   (client map: slot 0 on A)
slot 0 starts moving to C; pay-103 has been copied
  GET pay-103 -> A: ASK 0 C -> ASKING, C: "value of pay-103"   (client map: slot 0 on A)
  GET pay-117 -> A: "value of pay-117"   (client map: slot 0 on A)
  GET pay-159 -> A: "value of pay-159"   (client map: slot 0 on A)
the rest are copied, and C owns slot 0
  GET pay-103 -> A: MOVED 0 C -> C: "value of pay-103"   (client map: slot 0 on C)
  GET pay-117 -> C: "value of pay-117"   (client map: slot 0 on C)
  GET pay-159 -> C: "value of pay-159"   (client map: slot 0 on C)

During the migration only the copied key costs a hop, and the client's map still says A, which is right for the two keys A still holds. After the migration, the first read gets MOVED, the map flips to C, and the next two reads go straight there. Every read returned its value. The model uses 16 slots and MD5; Redis uses 16,384 slots and CRC16, with the same replies.

refs.title: Redis Cluster specification: MOVED and ASK redirection
MongoDB manual: sharded cluster query routing (mongos)

analogy: Picture a storage building with 1,000 numbered lockers and ten attendants. A customer's locker number is stamped on their key and never changes. When an eleventh attendant starts, the manager hands over the keys to 90 lockers from the other ten, a few from each; no locker moves and no customer gets a new number. A building that instead sends customer number c to attendant c mod N would make nearly every customer find a new attendant the day one is hired. To get served, a customer can ask any attendant, who walks them over; ask at the front desk; or carry a map. A customer with an old map hears "not me any more, she has it now" (MOVED), or, during a handover, "that locker has already gone to her, just this once" (ASK). The analogy breaks on cost: handing over a locker key takes a second, while moving a partition copies gigabytes between live machines, and the copying itself loads the very nodes it's meant to relieve.
world: Your Kafka topics are fixed partitions. A payments topic keyed by merchant gets its partition count once, and adding partitions later sends a merchant's new events to a different partition from its old ones, so the per-merchant order your consumers rely on breaks across the change. Pick the count with divisors in mind: 12 partitions spread evenly over 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12 consumers in a group, while with 5 consumers two of them get three partitions and three get two. The Kafka client already follows a redirect much like MOVED: when a broker restarts and leadership moves, the producer gets a not-leader error, refreshes its metadata and resends. With Redis Cluster through Lettuce, turn on adaptive topology refresh so that MOVED and ASK replies trigger a map refresh promptly. And if you ever shard Postgres or Oracle by hand, start with many logical shards on few machines, as Notion did.
mistake: The most common mistake is choosing the partition count for today's size. A topic created with 6 partitions is fine until the consumer group needs 12 members, and an index created with 3 primary shards is fine until each shard holds 200 GB. Raising the count later rehashes keys, which breaks per-key order in Kafka and means a split or a reindex in Elasticsearch. It happens because a small count looks tidy and the growth is years away. The fix is to size for the volume you expect in a few years, with a count that has many divisors (48, 60, 120, 480), and to check the per-partition overhead against your platform's guidance before going much higher.

worked.title: Choose the number of logical shards for a sharded ledger

steps.say: Start from the growth, not from today's machines. The ledger has 3 TB, grows 40 GB a day, and each Postgres machine should hold at most 500 GB.
steps.code:
today        3 TB                       -> 6 machines at 500 GB
in 3 years   3 TB + 40 GB x 1,095 days  = about 46.8 TB
             46.8 TB / 500 GB          -> about 94 machines

steps.say: So the count must spread evenly over anything from 6 to about 100 machines, with at least a few shards per machine at the top end so one machine can be relieved by moving one or two shards. Compare candidates by the busiest machine's share against the average.
steps.code: fun busiestVsAverage(partitions: Int, machines: Int): Double { val busiest = (partitions + machines - 1) / machines // ceil(P / N) return busiest / (partitions.toDouble() / machines) } for (p in listOf(256, 480, 512, 720)) println("$p: " + listOf(6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 96).map { "%.2f".format(busiestVsAverage(p, it)) })

steps.say: Read the result. 480 is perfectly even at every count from 6 to 96 machines. 720 is uneven at 32 and 96 (720 / 96 = 7.5, so some machines hold 8 and some 7). 256 and 512 are even only at powers of two, and at 96 machines the busiest carries 13% more than the average. Pick 480.

Keep the routing table small and in one place. Each logical shard is a schema; the table maps shard number to a database host. Moving a shard is: copy the schema to the new host, catch up from the old host's replication stream, pause writes to that one shard for a moment, flip the table entry, resume. Every other shard keeps working.
steps.code: const val LOGICAL_SHARDS = 480 fun logicalShard(merchantId: String): Int = Math.floorMod(stableHash(merchantId), LOGICAL_SHARDS.toLong()).toInt() // never changes // the second map: logical shard -> host, kept in one store every router reads val hostOf: Map<Int, String> = (0 until LOGICAL_SHARDS).associateWith { "ledger-db-%02d".format(it % 6) }

lab.title: Rebalance two ways, then follow MOVED and ASK
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. 13 of 15 fail with NotImplementedError. Two pass already: the hash mod N count, which uses the given ModN, and the importing node's reply without ASKING, which tests the given Cluster.

In Placement.kt, write FixedPartitions.addNode: move one partition at a time from the busiest node to the new one until it holds its fair share. Watch the jqwik property: for any node count and partition count, every node ends with the fair share rounded down or up.

In DynamicRanges.kt, write insert: add the key to its range, and split a range that passes maxKeys at its median key. The test with time-ordered keys checks that every insert lands in the last range, however often it splits.
In Redirects.kt, write RoutingClient.get: follow MOVED (update the map) and ASK (one request with asking = true, map unchanged). All 15 pass.

Experiment: change your Ask branch so it also writes the new node into slotMap. Run the tests and read which one fails, and why: the client now sends the keys still on A to C, which bounces them back with MOVED. Put it back.
hints: addNode: count partitions per node first (owner.forEach { counts.merge(it, 1, Int::plus) }), then loop while the new node holds fewer than partitionCount / nodes.size. The donor is the max by count, then by name sorting first: compareBy<Map.Entry<String, Int>> { it.value }.thenByDescending { it.key }.
The donor's highest partition is owner.indices.last { owner[it] == donor }.

insert: range.keys.elementAt(range.keys.size / 2) is the median. range.keys.tailSet(median, true) is a live view of the upper half: copy it into the new range's keys, then clear() the view to remove those keys from the old range. Put the new range in byStart under the median.
get: loop at most six times. Keep node and asking in local variables. On Moved, set slotMap[reply.slot] = reply.node and asking = false; on Ask, set asking = true and touch nothing else.

drill.title: The redirect loop from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write get(key) for a client with a slotMap: Array<String> and a send(node, key, asking): Reply, where Reply is Value(v), Moved(slot, node) or Ask(slot, node). Then say in one sentence why Ask must not update the map.

answer.html: fun get(key: String): String? { var node = slotMap[slotOf(key)] var asking = false repeat(6) { when (val r = send(node, key, asking)) { is Reply.Value -> return r.value is Reply.Moved -> { slotMap[r.slot] = r.node; node = r.node; asking = false } // the slot moved for good is Reply.Ask -> { node = r.node; asking = true } // this key, this once } } throw IllegalStateException("too many redirects for $key") } // During a migration most of the slot's keys are still on the old owner; // pointing the map at the new owner would bounce all of them back with MOVED.

recap: hash mod N moves about N/(N+1) of the keys when a node joins (91% going from 10 to 11). A good scheme moves about 1/(N+1), all of it to the new node, from many senders.

Fixed partitions (Kafka, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch, Redis Cluster's 16,384 slots, Notion's 480) hash keys to P partitions once and move whole partitions. Choose P big and with many divisors: it's hard to change later.

Key-range stores split ranges as they grow (HBase at 10 GiB, CockroachDB at 512 MiB and when a range gets too busy; MongoDB's balancer works in 128 MB ranges). Cassandra's partition count grows with the nodes, 16 ranges each.
Automatic rebalancing can cascade: an overloaded node is called dead, its load lands on the others, and they fail in turn. Keep a person in the loop for membership, and rebalance before a known peak.

Requests find shards through any node (Cassandra), a routing tier (mongos, DBProxy, Vitess) or a partition-aware client (token-aware drivers, Kafka metadata, Redis Cluster). The authoritative map lives in a consensus store or is spread by gossip.
Redis Cluster's MOVED updates the client's map; ASK sends one request, after ASKING, to the importing node and leaves the map alone. No request fails during a migration.

explain.prompt: Your team shards the ledger over 8 Postgres machines with hash(merchant_id) mod 8 and now needs 4 more machines. Explain why that's painful, and what you'd have done differently.
explain.answer: With hash mod 8, going to 12 machines changes the remainder for most merchants: a merchant stays only if its hash leaves the same remainder mod 8 and mod 12, which happens for 8 out of every 24 hash values, a third. So about two thirds of the data has to be copied, much of it between old machines that aren't gaining anything, all while serving payments. And during the move, every router has to know which merchants have moved, merchant by merchant. If we'd started with fixed logical shards, say 480 schemas with 60 on each of the 8 machines, a merchant's logical shard would never change. Adding 4 machines would move 160 whole schemas, 40 to each new machine, a third of the data, all of it to new machines, and the routing table would change one schema at a time. 480 also spreads evenly over 8, 12, 16 or 24 machines. We'd keep that table in one place every router reads, and move shards one at a time by hand, outside the peak season.

deeper.html:
Rebalancing tools have become first-class operations in the stores you'll use.

MongoDB 8.0 added moveCollection (move an unsharded collection to another shard), unshardCollection, and resharding to the same shard key as a way to redistribute data. Resharding writes to all shards in parallel, while the balancer's chunk migrations are limited to one per shard at a time; Percona measured a few-gigabyte reshard at about 3 minutes on MongoDB 7.0 and under 1 minute on 8.0, on an idle cluster.

Redis 8.4 and Valkey 9.0 added atomic slot migration, which moves a whole slot as one operation instead of key by key. Clients still have to understand MOVED, but the window in which ASK appears shrinks.

Elasticsearch and OpenSearch can split an index into a multiple of its primary shard count, or shrink it to a factor of it, without reindexing every document. Any other change of the shard count is a reindex.

Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 7 has a good section on the open problems of request routing: who decides the assignment without split brain, how routers learn about changes, and what happens to requests in flight at the cutover. The Consistency and consensus track answers the first question; this lesson's MOVED and ASK are one answer to the third.
